newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD draws flak over new tax proposal.
newsitem.headline: German SPD draws flak over new tax proposal.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrats (SPD) on Saturday announced details of a long-awaited tax reform policy but ran into sniping from the government which accused them of zigzagging on key issues.
Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition SPD, told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper that his party's tax proposals would make the average wage earner 2,500 marks ($1,500) a year better off.
Lafontaine told Bild in an interview due to be published on Sunday the SPD was ready to negotiate a modest cut in top-rate income tax and make step-by-step cuts in the entry rate.
"We want a tax reform which comes into force from January 1, 1998. Our reform would bring a noticeable net cut in taxes for workers," Lafontaine said.
The SPD, which will unveil its plan on Monday, has wrangled for months over tax policy.
Its lack of a clear position on key issues was blamed by many for the failure of talks with the government earlier this year aimed at pinning down a compromise.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel reacted quickly, accusing the SPD of a "weekly tax slalom".

With Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government controlling only one of two houses of parliament, the two sides must produce a compromise to avoid an SPD veto before the window of opportunity is closed by next year's general election.

Although Waigel has not ruled out emergency tax hikes to get the budget deficit down this year and qualify for European monetary union, all sides are talking about cutting tax to help the economy in the long term.
But they disagree on key points.
Waigel has brought legislation into parliament which would trim corporate taxes next year before launching sweeping income tax cuts in 1999, to be offset by scrapping over 70 tax breaks.

His tax bills would relieve the German taxpayer by a net 30 billion marks a year by cutting the top rate of income tax to 39 percent from 53 percent and lowering the entry rate to 15 percent from 26 percent now.
Lafontaine also proposes cutting the entry rate of tax to 15 percent eventually, starting with a reduction to 22 percent next year.
He also said the top-rate tax could fall to 45 percent -- a comment mocked by Waigel who noted that Lafontaine had refused to agree to tax cuts for the rich in the past.

"In presenting the opposition's long-awaited tax concept the party leader has finally been caught up by reality," Waigel told the newspaper Welt am Sonntag in remarks also released ahead of publication on Sunday.
Lafontaine said he also wanted to raise tax allowances by 2,000 marks to 14,000 marks for single earners, and up monthly child allowances to 250 marks.
A two-point cut in social security charges this October would also create 200,000 jobs.
The two sides are closer on cutting corporate taxes, with the SPD ready to drop the rate on retained profits to 35 percent from 45.
Lafontaine said he was also ready to bow to government pressure to scrap a corporate capital trading tax, something the SPD has blocked in parliament for two years.
But each harbours deep suspicions over the other side's counter-financing measures.
The SPD sees a real gap of over 50 billion marks in Waigel's plan. The finance minister retorted that the SPD's arithmetic was "extremely dubious".
Waigel wants to raise value-added tax to pay for part of the cuts in direct tax cuts.
The SPD, in another change of position, would also raise VAT by one point to 16 percent and raise petrol tax by six pfennigs per litre, the daily Die Welt said.
